introduction-its-not-just-a-text-editor.core: VS Code is a platform: language servers, debuggers, remote development, terminals and extensions turn it into an environment for writing, running and debugging code wherever it lives.

first_principles.problem: Using VS Code as a plain text editor leaves debugging, remote editing and automation on the table.
truths: Ops work spans languages and machines.
Context switching between tools costs focus.
An extensible platform adapts to each workflow.

analogy.title: A smartphone vs. a landline
analogy.story: Both make calls; one also navigates, photographs and runs apps.
analogy.breaks: Power features need setup. Out of the box it's just an editor.

example.title: An ops engineer's day
example.outcome: the IDE becomes a force multiplier.

check.q: What makes VS Code more than a text editor?
check.a: Its extensible platform: language servers, debug adapters, remote development and extensions.

the-vs-code-architecture-why-it-can-do-a.core: VS Code splits a UI client from extension hosts and protocol servers: the Language Server Protocol for intelligence and the Debug Adapter Protocol for debugging. The heavy work can run anywhere: locally, over SSH or in a container.

first_principles.problem: Monolithic editors need custom integrations for every language and can't run tooling remotely.
truths: Protocols decouple editors from language tooling.
UI and computation can be separated.
derivation: A **remote server** runs extensions next to the code.

analogy.title: A TV remote and a set-top box
analogy.story: The remote (UI) is in your hand; the box (server) does the work and can sit anywhere it's connected.
analogy.breaks: Network latency to a remote server can make the UI feel sluggish.

example.title: Go-to-definition in a remote Go repo
flow: Request → VS Code Server on host

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: The code and tools never leave the server.

example.outcome: you understand why remote development and multi-language support work.

check.a: How editors talk to language tools for completion, diagnostics and navigation.

debugging-configurations-launchjson.core: launch.json defines how to start or attach a debugger (program, args, env, cwd), so you can set breakpoints and inspect variables, the call stack and conditions instead of sprinkling print statements.

first_principles.problem: Debugging by print statement takes many edit-run cycles and still misses state.
truths: Pausing execution reveals the full state.
Attaching to running processes needs configuration.

analogy.title: Pausing a film to examine a frame
analogy.story: Instead of guessing from the trailer, you freeze the frame and see every detail.
analogy.breaks: Debuggers can change timing, so concurrency bugs may hide under the debugger.

example.title: Debugging a CLI with args

steps.label: Use
steps.detail: Press F5, hit the breakpoint and inspect the config dict.

example.outcome: bugs are found by inspection, not guesswork.

check.a: A breakpoint that logs a message without pausing execution.

remote-development-ssh-and-containers.core: Remote-SSH and Dev Containers run VS Code's server where the code actually runs. You edit, debug and use terminals with the target's exact runtime, files and network.

first_principles.problem: A script works on the laptop but fails on the server because of a different Python, missing libraries or network access.
truths: Copying files back and forth is slow and error-prone.
Editing with vim over SSH lacks IDE features.
derivation: **Remote-SSH**: connect to a host, and the server runs there.
**Dev Containers**: open the folder inside a container.

analogy.title: Remote-controlling a robot on site
analogy.story: You operate from your desk with full controls, but the work happens at the real site.
analogy.breaks: It needs connectivity and server resources, and some extensions don't work remotely.

example.title: Debugging on a bastion host
example.outcome: development happens in the real environment.

check.q: Where do extensions like the Python language server run under Remote-SSH?
check.a: On the remote host, next to the code.

extensions-management.core: Extensions cost memory, CPU and startup time, and they're a supply-chain risk. Keep a curated set, use workspace recommendations and profiles, and disable per-workspace whatever you don't need.

first_principles.problem: Fifty installed extensions make VS Code slow, and a malicious extension could read your credentials.

analogy.title: Apps on your phone
analogy.story: Every app drains battery and can see data, so you keep the useful ones and remove the rest.
analogy.breaks: Recommendations are suggestions, and users can still install anything.

steps.label: Tip
steps.detail: Use 'Extension Bisect' to find the extension slowing things down.

check.q: What feature helps find a misbehaving extension?
check.a: Extension Bisect, which disables half the extensions repeatedly to isolate the culprit.

snippets-and-productivity-shortcuts.core: Snippets expand short prefixes into templated boilerplate with tab stops, and keyboard shortcuts (command palette, multi-cursor, quick open) remove repetitive typing and mouse trips.

first_principles.problem: Typing the same Terraform resource or Kubernetes manifest skeleton by hand is slow and invites typos.
truths: Keyboard actions are faster than menus.

analogy.title: Speed-dial and stamps
analogy.story: Instead of dialling the whole number or handwriting the address, you press one key or use a stamp.
analogy.breaks: Too many snippets are forgotten, so keep the ones you actually use.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Three keystrokes produce a correct skeleton.

check.q: What does ${1:name} mean in a snippet?
check.a: The first tab stop, with placeholder text 'name'.
